European Parliament · ninth term · plenary speeches

European Parliament 2019–2024

The speeches

Every speech in the plenary of the European Parliament is published in the language it was given. The data comes with an English version: the original for speeches given in English, otherwise a machine translation. All analyses use the English text, so speeches in 24 languages can be compared. Speeches by the President, the Commission and the Council are left out, as are procedural items (agenda, voting time, minutes).

Group agendas: who talks about what

Lift is a group's share of speeches in a domain divided by the share across the whole Parliament. Above 1 (orange) means the group speaks about the domain more than average; below 1 (blue) less. Groups are ordered from left to right.

Most distinctive topics

Where groups stand on contested issues

For nine issues that divide the Parliament, a local language model read speeches on the issue (up to 25 per group) and judged whether the speaker argues for or against a statement. A group's position is (for − against) / (for + against). Choose an issue to see the national parties within the groups: this is where groups split.

−1 every speech against0 balanced+1 every speech for Dot size: speeches

National parties with at least six speeches on the issue in the sample. The sample was drawn per group, so small parties in large groups are often missing.

Countries: what MEPs from each member state talk about

The same lift, now by the member state an MEP represents. Choose a domain to colour the map; hover over a country for its most distinctive topics.

Most distinctive topics

Regions named in the debates

Place names in the speeches were found with named entity recognition and looked up in a gazetteer of all towns and cities of the EU (GeoNames). Each place lies in a NUTS 2 region. The map counts the speeches that name a place in the region; choose a domain to see where the Parliament looks when it talks about, for example, migration.

The outermost regions (Canary Islands, Azores, Madeira, French overseas departments) are not drawn.

Which group names which country

Sustainability: the Sustainable Development Goals in the debates

To follow sustainability as a whole, every speech was compared with short descriptions of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals (zero-shot classification on the same sentence embeddings). A speech gets the closest goal if it is similar enough; the threshold was chosen by reading the speeches just above it. The eight environmental goals (food and farming, water, energy, cities, consumption, climate, seas and land) are in green.

Share of speeches by goal

Goal 16 (peace and justice) almost never reaches the threshold: its description is broad, and speeches on the rule of law or human rights are closer to other goals, or to none. The descriptions shape the result.

Climate and energy, by quarter

Energy rises from late 2021, when gas prices first went up, and peaks after the Russian invasion of Ukraine (24 February 2022).

How groups frame climate and energy

Words per 1,000 in speeches on climate action and clean energy, from three dictionaries: cost (costs, burden, affordable, competitiveness, bureaucracy, households, job losses), urgency (emergency, urgent, catastrophe, future generations, planet, science) and opportunity (opportunity, innovation, green jobs, investment, leadership, growth). A dictionary is blunt: a speech can name costs to argue that inaction costs more.

Organisations in the debates

Organisations named in the speeches (named entity recognition), without the Parliament's own groups and the EU institutions. Agencies, international organisations, companies, NGOs and national institutions.
